lesson.title: Measure it right
lesson.subtitle: Read the scale, write it down, catch the mistakes

video.title: Measure it right
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Narrator — the Darsi voice (warm, peer to peer)

scenes.visual: Ms Salma at the board, arms folded, looking at three numbers written by three students: 70, 700, 28. One desk in front of her.
scenes.animation: The three numbers appear one by one; she raises an eyebrow.
scenes.narration: Three of my students measured the same desk. Kemi wrote seventy. Tunde wrote seven hundred. Grace wrote twenty-eight. Funny thing is, they could all be right.

scenes.visual: Darsi title card with the IoT track chip.
scenes.animation: Mark pops in; title slides up.
scenes.narration: Today: measure it right, write it down well, and catch readings that can't be true.

scenes.visual: Three tapes laid along the same desk: a ruler in centimetres, a ruler in millimetres, a tailor's tape in inches. All end at the same edge.
scenes.animation: Each tape slides along the desk as it is named; the ends line up.
scenes.narration: Look at their tapes. Kemi measured seventy centimetres. Tunde measured seven hundred millimetres: the same length. Grace used a tailor's tape in inches: about twenty-eight. A number without its unit means almost nothing.

scenes.visual: Two scales side by side: one from 20 to 30 with ten small gaps, one from 0 to 20 with four small gaps. The gaps light up as they are counted.
scenes.animation: Gaps light up one at a time; the worth of each appears beside it.
scenes.on_screen_text: What is each small gap worth?
scenes.narration: Next, read the scale. Find two numbered marks, and count the small gaps between them. Ten gaps from twenty to thirty? Each gap is worth one. Four gaps from zero to twenty? Each is worth five.

scenes.visual: An eye beside a measuring cylinder: level with the water, a check; above and below, a cross. The water's curved surface, with a line at its lowest point.
scenes.animation: The eye moves up, level, down; the check and crosses pop in.
scenes.narration: Then bring your eye level with the mark. Look from above or below, and you'll line up the wrong mark. With water in a tube, read at the bottom of its curved surface.

scenes.visual: Mr Okafor at his lab bench holds up a measuring cylinder: 10 and 20 marked, five small gaps between, water three gaps above 10. Three answer cards drop in.
scenes.animation: Cards drop in with a small bounce.
scenes.narration: Quick check! My measuring cylinder has five small gaps between ten and twenty millilitres. The water is three gaps above ten. What's the reading?

scenes.visual: The cylinder again: each of the five gaps gets a small label '2'; three are counted above 10; the reading 16 lights up. A '13' card gets a cross.
scenes.animation: Labels pop on each gap; the count ticks up to 16.
scenes.narration: Sixteen millilitres. Ten millilitres across five gaps makes each gap worth two. Three gaps is six, and ten plus six is sixteen. Thirteen is the trap: it counts every gap as one.

scenes.visual: A notebook page: one line written neatly with four coloured parts: 31, °C, 2 pm, back of the classroom.
scenes.animation: Each part writes itself on in turn.
scenes.narration: Now write it down. A good record has four parts: number, unit, time and place. Thirty-one degrees Celsius, two in the afternoon, back of the classroom. Without a time and place, nobody can compare it later.

scenes.visual: A bar chart of five school days; the middle bar shoots far above the others.
scenes.animation: Bars grow one by one; the tall bar wobbles.
scenes.on_screen_text: A reading that can't be right
scenes.narration: Sometimes a reading can't be right. Here's a week of classroom temperatures: twenty-eight, twenty-nine, then eighty-five! No classroom gets that hot. With it, the week's average is forty degrees. Without it, about twenty-nine.

scenes.visual: The 85 in a notebook gets a ring, not a rubbing-out; beside it a note: 'glitch? loose wire'. A second thermometer is held up next to the first.
scenes.animation: The ring draws round 85; the note writes itself on.
scenes.on_screen_text: Check it, mark it, explain it
scenes.narration: A reading like that is a glitch: maybe a loose wire, or a slip of the pen. Don't rub it out, and don't just trust it. Measure again, or check with another tool. Then mark it, keep it, and note why you left it out.

scenes.visual: Amina in the school garden beside a soil sensor on a stick; a phone shows 50, 0, 50. Three answer cards bounce in.
scenes.animation: Cards bounce in one by one.
scenes.on_screen_text: What do you do with the 0?
scenes.narration: Your turn. The garden's soil moisture sensor reads fifty percent, then exactly zero at midnight, then fifty again an hour later. What do you do with that zero?

scenes.visual: Three icons line up: a ruler, a notebook line, a ringed number.
scenes.narration: Mark it, keep it and check the wires: soil doesn't dry out and get wet again in an hour. Remember: the unit, the gap, eye level. Number, unit, time and place. And check readings that can't be right.

scenes.visual: Two students measure the same desk with a ruler and write a small table; they compare and one points to a unit.
scenes.animation: Rows fill in the table one by one.
scenes.narration: Try it tomorrow: measure your desk three times, the same way each time. Write each reading with its number, unit, time and place. Then compare with a friend, and if you disagree, find out why. Next time: connected things, safely.

checkpoints.prompt: 5 small gaps between 10 and 20 mL, and the water is 3 gaps above 10. What's the reading?
checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — 10 mL across 5 gaps makes each gap 2 mL, so 3 gaps are 6 mL and the reading is 16 mL.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — each gap here is worth 2 mL, not 1, because 5 gaps share 10 mL. Three gaps are 6 mL, so the reading is 16 mL.

checkpoints.prompt: Soil moisture: 50 %, then exactly 0 at midnight, then 50 an hour later. What do you do with the 0?

options.text: Mark it, keep it, check the wires
Delete it so the graph looks clean
Water the garden at once: it's dry

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — soil can't dry out and get wet again in an hour with nobody watering. It's a glitch, often a loose wire: mark it, keep it, and check.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — deleting hides the problem, and watering trusts a reading that can't be true. Soil doesn't dry out and come back in an hour: mark the glitch and check the wires.
